results.title: Google Labs: The Experimental Playground I’ve Been Ignoring for Way Too Long | by Gokul Suresh | Medium
results.content:
By ignoring Labs, I was essentially saying “I don’t care about seeing the future before it arrives.”

That was short-sighted.

## Resources and Next Steps

If you want to explore Google Labs yourself:

Official Links:

 Main Labs portal: labs.google
 Jules documentation: jules.google/docs
 Stitch: stitch.withgoogle.com
 Sign up for experiments: blog.google/technology/ai/google-labs-sign-up

Stay Updated:

 Google Labs newsletter
 Follow @GoogleLabs on X/Twitter
 Join the Google Labs Discord and Reddit communities

Alternative: Experiments with Google For a broader view of Google’s experimental projects beyond Labs, check out experiments.withgoogle.com — it includes work from Chrome, Android, AI, AR, and more.

## Final Thoughts [...] Here’s my approach after finally diving in:

1. Set realistic expectations These aren’t replacements for production tools. They’re supplements for specific use cases where being cutting-edge matters more than being stable.

2. Start with low-risk experiments Try Jules on a personal project before your company’s main repository. Test Stitch for internal mockups before client deliverables.

3. Give detailed feedback The entire point of Labs is iteration. If something doesn’t work, report it. If something works brilliantly, tell them what you were trying to do.

4. Track what graduates Pay attention to which experiments get promoted to full products. That tells you where Google is placing long-term bets. [...] ## Whisk: Visual Remixing with AI

Whisk lets you prompt with images for a fast and fun creative process. Instead of writing detailed text prompts, you drag in images for the subject, scene, and style, and Whisk remixes them.

Technical process: Whisk uses Gemini to automatically write a detailed caption of your images, which is then fed into Imagen 3 to generate the final image.

Philosophy: In early testing with artists and creatives, people have been describing Whisk as a new type of creative tool — not a traditional image editor. It was built for rapid visual exploration, not pixel-perfect edits.

This is important: Whisk doesn’t replace Photoshop or Figma. It’s for the ideation phase, when you’re exploring concepts quickly rather than perfecting final assets.

results.title: Google Playground Lets You Build Games—No Coding
results.content:
Summary

Google launched Playground, an experimental web platform that uses Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria models to turn text prompts into playable 2D and 3D browser games. Available to US adults with tiered creation tokens linked to Google One, Playground supports multi-turn editing, public gallery sharing, and an upcoming Unity Spark integration for advanced mechanics.

Google Labs is diving into game development with its latest public experiment. The Google team just launched Playground, a web platform that lets anyone build, test, and share browser games using AI simply by describing what they want in a chat box—no coding background or complex software engines required.

### 4. Google Vids

Google Vids is a hybrid of a video editor and Google Slides that lets you create animated presentations with visuals, transitions, etc. Just last week, Google added the ability to insert AI avatars and create image-to-video clips%20that%20can%20turn%20photos%20and%20scripts%20into%20narrated%20clips.).

> Daniel’s take: While it has potential as a more engaging alternative to Google Slides, the free version of Google Vids is quite limited. For most AI-powered features like animated avatars and Veo-powered video clips, you’ll need to upgrade.

### 5. ImageFX

ImageFX is a simple text-to-image playground where you generate images from a prompt. It gives you several minor controls, like setting the aspect ratio or keeping the seed fixed for repeatable generations. [...] > Daniel’s take: Illuminiate doesn’t do much more than what you can already achieve with NotebookLM (which also lets you work with multiple sources at once). But if you are only interested in a single source, want to skip a few steps, and need a bit more control over the end result, Illuminate is a great alternative.

### 28. Learn About

Learn About lets you explore any topic or question by generating an on-the-fly curriculum and learning path with vetted sources, complete with chapters and quizzes. You can dive deeper into specifics, request simpler explanations, or ask open-ended follow-up questions.

# If you can think it, you can play it.

## Introducing Playground, an experimental gaming platform where you can create custom games in minutes, no coding required.

Stop dreaming of games and start making them. With Playground, you can create custom games in minutes using simple text prompts, no coding experience required. Whether you’re a hobbyist with a notebook full of ideas or just curious about AI, our chat-based interface makes it easy to bring your vision to life. Choose from popular genres like Trivia, Tower Defense, and Racing, or create from scratch. It's your game, you make the rules.

Playground is designed to turn ideas into playable games without requiring users to write code.   
  
Google says users can describe what they want to build and experiment with creating their own interactive gaming experiences, lowering the technical barrier for people who want to develop games.  
  
The project is currently an experiment from Google Labs and is available to users ages 18 and older in the United States.   
  
Playground is another example of Google exploring how generative AI can make software and game creation accessible to people without traditional programming experience.
